stem:
The Venus fly trap, *Dionaea muscipula*, is a carnivorous plant, native to wetlands of the East Coast of the USA. Mineral ions from decayed organisms are often washed away in these wetlands.

Fig. 7.1 shows a Venus fly trap leaf.

{{figure:figure_7_1.webp}}

Fig. 7.1

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Suggest why a Venus fly trap benefits from catching insects in these wetlands.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text:
The leaves of the Venus fly trap will close if stimulated by an insect.

State which part of the leaf detects the stimulus.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Explain how the plant does not waste energy by closing when it does not need to, such as when a large drop of rain touches the receptor.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
Fig. 7.2 is a graph of an action potential in a human neurone.

{{figure:figure_7_2.webp}}

Fig. 7.2

Fig. 7.3 is a graph of an action potential in leaf cells of a Venus fly trap.

{{figure:figure_7_3.webp}}

Fig. 7.3

With reference to Fig. 7.2 and Fig. 7.3, describe how the action potential of the Venus fly trap differs from that of a human.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Describe how the production of action potentials in the leaf cells of the Venus fly trap can result in the leaves closing and trapping an insect.
